docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: This section explains the ideas behind the POSTED data model. It describes what the pieces of a techno-economic data file mean and why they are structured as they are. The precise file format is specified in Format, and the processing steps are described in NO-SL-AG.

docs.title: Raw data and harmonised data
docs.text:
POSTED distinguishes strictly between two representations of the same data.

Raw data is what contributors enter into the database. Every row of a TEDF records one value together with the context in which the source reports it: the unit, the quantity it refers to, the year, the sub-technology, the source, and the position within the source. The guiding rule is to stay as close to the original publication as possible. If a report states an investment cost of 1566 EUR per kg of hydrogen per day in 2020 prices, that is what the row contains, even if other sources use EUR per kW or USD per tonne per year.

Harmonised data is what the framework produces from raw data. All values of a variable are expressed in one unit and relative to one reference quantity, currencies are deflated to one base year, variants of a variable are mapped onto a canonical form, and values are interpolated to the requested years. Harmonised data from different sources is directly comparable and can be averaged.

This separation has consequences for how the database is maintained. Contributors never convert values by hand, because every conversion would hide an assumption that cannot be checked later. When a source reports a value in a form that cannot be expressed directly, e.g. a cost per tonne of steel where the TEDF is about direct reduced iron, the conversion is recorded in the comment column so that it remains traceable. Where a conversion is systematic, e.g. from full-load hours to a capacity factor, it is implemented once in the framework as a variable mapping rather than being repeated by every contributor.

docs.title: Variables and reference variables
docs.text:
A variable names the quantity that a row reports. Variable names are hierarchical, with segments separated by a vertical bar, e.g. CAPEX, Input|Electricity, or Output Capacity|Hydrogen. The leading part of the hierarchy, the parent variable, is given by the position of the TEDF in the database rather than being repeated in each row. The row Input|Electricity in the file tedfs/Tech/Electrolysis.csv therefore stands for Tech|Electrolysis|Input|Electricity.

Many techno-economic parameters are ratios. A specific investment cost is a cost per unit of capacity, an energy demand is an energy input per unit of product, an emission intensity is a mass of CO2 per unit of output. POSTED represents such ratios explicitly by splitting them into two variables.

  • The variable is the numerator, e.g. CAPEX or Input|Electricity.
  • The reference variable is the denominator, e.g. Output Capacity|Hydrogen or Output|Hydrogen.

Each half has its own value and unit. A row may therefore state that 1566 EUR of CAPEX corresponds to 1 kg of hydrogen output capacity per day, or that 541 cubic metres of hydrogen are consumed per 1.1 tonnes of direct reduced iron. This representation serves three purposes.

  1. Faithfulness. Sources report ratios in many ways, and the two-part representation can store all of them without conversion.
  2. Unit handling. Numerator and denominator are converted separately, so a cost in EUR per kg of hydrogen per day can be converted to EUR per kW of hydrogen output by converting only the denominator.
  3. Rebasing. When several sources refer their data to different quantities, e.g. one to hydrogen output and another to electricity input, the framework can rebase all of them onto one common reference using the conversion ratios that the same source provides.

Variable definitions classify how a variable relates to its reference. Three kinds matter for processing.

  • Activity-type variables describe flows during operation and are reported per unit of another flow, e.g. energy inputs per unit of product or variable OPEX per unit of product. Their reference variable is itself a flow, e.g. Output|Hydrogen.
  • Capacity-type variables describe quantities tied to the installed plant and are reported per unit of capacity, e.g. CAPEX or fixed OPEX. Their reference variable is a capacity, e.g. Output Capacity|Hydrogen.
  • Intensive variables are dimensionless or self-contained and have no reference variable, e.g. a lifetime, a capacity factor, or a capture rate.

In harmonised data, all activity-type variables of a TEDF share one reference activity and all capacity-type variables share one reference capacity. The framework determines these by default as the most common reference variables found in the data. They can also be set explicitly, e.g. to express an electrolyser's data per unit of electricity input rather than per unit of hydrogen output.

docs.title: Cases and components
docs.text:
Techno-economic data for one technology rarely consists of a single number per variable. Sources distinguish sub-technologies, plant sizes, operating modes, regions, and years. They also break quantities down into parts, e.g. investment cost into equipment and installation, or hydrogen demand into reduction agent and heating.

POSTED represents each such distinction as a field, i.e. an additional column in the TEDF. Fields come in two types that differ in what the entries mean in relation to each other.

  • Case fields hold competing alternatives. The values in a case field are different answers to the same question, e.g. alkaline versus PEM electrolysis, a 1 MW versus a 100 MW plant, or the year 2030 versus 2050. Only one of them applies at a time. When data is aggregated over a case field, the values are averaged, because they are alternative estimates of the same quantity.
  • Component fields hold parts of a whole. The values in a component field are contributions that together make up the reported quantity, e.g. several cost items that add up to the total fixed OPEX. When data is aggregated over a component field, the values are summed.

The source column is present in every TEDF and is treated as a case field, because different sources are competing estimates of the same quantity. The period column is a predefined case field that most TEDFs declare, because the same quantity in different years represents alternative points in time. Whether a TEDF needs further fields, and which, is decided per technology and declared in its metadata. The electrolysis TEDF, for instance, distinguishes subtech, size, and country. The TEDF for direct reduction of iron distinguishes carbon_capture and mode as case fields and has a component field.

The distinction between cases and components also informs how missing information is encoded. A source may report a value that holds for all alternatives of a case, which is recorded with an asterisk (*). A source may fail to state which alternative a value refers to, which is recorded as not specified (N/S). A source may report a total without breaking it into components, which is recorded with a hash (#) in the component field. The Format section defines these entries, and the NO-SL-AG section explains how they are resolved when data is selected.

docs.title: Periods
docs.text: The period field records the year a value refers to. For historical data this is the year of the estimate. For projections it is the target year of the projection. Periods behave like any other case field with one addition: because years are ordered, the framework can interpolate between reported years and extrapolate beyond them. A request for the year 2035 can thus be served from a source that reports 2030 and 2040. This treatment is configurable and can be switched off.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Every row of a TEDF names exactly one source, identified by a BibTeX key that is defined in the sources.bib file of the database. A second column, source_detail, records where within the source the value can be found, e.g. a table, page, or spreadsheet cell. Together they allow each number in the database to be traced back to its origin.

The source is itself a case field. Aggregating over sources means averaging the estimates of different publications, which is the default behaviour of the aggregation step. Sources can also be used to restrict a selection, e.g. to compare only two particular studies, or to weight and exclude entries through masks.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
A database is a directory containing TEDFs, their metadata, variable definitions, variable mappings, masks, and the BibTeX file of sources. POSTED ships one public database inside the package. Additional databases, e.g. for project-specific or confidential data, can be registered at runtime and are read with the same code paths.

The public database is intended for a comprehensive set of general-purpose data that serves most users. Private databases provide a low-threshold way to extend POSTED without going through the review process of the public database, and they allow working with data that cannot be published.

docs.title: Variable mappings
docs.text:
Sources express the same information in different forms. One source gives fixed operating cost as a percentage of CAPEX, another as an absolute cost per unit of capacity, a third as a cost per unit of product. One source gives the utilisation of a plant as full-load hours, another as a capacity factor. Harmonised data must express each of these in one canonical form.

POSTED handles such cases with variable mappings: small pieces of code, stored in the database, that transform one representation of a variable into another during the selection step. A mapping is applied uniformly to all data in a TEDF, so the transformation is documented once and applied consistently. Some mappings need other variables from the same source and case, e.g. the CAPEX to convert a relative OPEX into an absolute one. If a required variable is missing, the framework issues a warning and drops the affected entry rather than guessing. The mappings of the public database are listed in the NO-SL-AG section.

docs.title: Masks
docs.text: Not every value in the database should enter every analysis. A source may be known to misquote another, or a user may prefer to weight recent sources more strongly. Rather than deleting such entries, which would destroy information, POSTED keeps them and lets the aggregation step decide. A mask assigns weights to rows that match a condition. A weight of zero or an undefined weight excludes a row, and intermediate weights produce a weighted average. Masks can be stored in the database as defaults for a TEDF or passed to the aggregation step by the user.

docs.title: Units and flows
docs.text:
Techno-economic data combines physical units, energy units, and currencies. Flows such as hydrogen or ammonia can be quantified by mass, by volume, or by energy content, and conversion between these depends on the substance and on conventions such as lower or higher heating value. Currencies additionally carry a base year.

POSTED delegates unit handling to the cet-units package, which extends the pint library with flow-specific units such as kg_H2 or MWh_NH3_LHV and with currencies such as EUR_2020. Normalisation converts all values of a variable to a single unit, including conversions between mass and energy for flows and deflation between currency years. The Units section describes the notation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Role in the data model Treatment in processing Parent variable Identifies a TEDF and prefixes its variables Optionally prepended to output Variable and reference variable Numerator and denominator of a reported ratio Converted separately, rebased onto common references Case field Competing alternatives, including source and period Selected by value, averaged when aggregated Component field Parts that add up to a whole Summed when aggregated Period Year of the estimate Interpolated and extrapolated on request Variable mapping Code converting one form of a variable into another Applied during selection Mask Weights for rows matching a condition Applied during aggregation Unit Physical unit, flow unit, or currency with base year Converted during normalisation

docs.title: How to contribute to POSTED
docs.text: Contributions to the data curated in POSTED and to the functionalities implemented in its code are very much encouraged and greatly appreciated.

docs.title: By creating a pull request on GitHub
docs.text:
POSTED — including its public database and the source code of its underlying Python framework — is managed on a public GitHub repository.

You can contribute your data directly by:

  • Forking POSTED on GitHub
  • Clone your fork and make local edits
  • Commit your changes to your forked repository
  • Create a pull request here

Generic information on creating pull requests can be found here.

This method has many advantages, e.g. automated testing procedures, discussing changes through the GitHub interface, full public transparency, etc.

docs.title: By sending a data file to the maintainers
docs.text:
GitHub pull requests may be a barrier for contribution to some users. We therefore also encourage users to send us their raw data directly.

Data files can be sent directly via email to philipp DOT verpoort AT pik MINUS potsdam DOT de (email address obfuscated to protect against web crawlers). Files can be attached directly to emails (if less than 10 MB in size) or uploaded to an appropriate file-sharing service. Files may be shared as comma-separated value (CSV) ASCII files, as XLSX files (typically created using Microsoft® Excel® or compatible software), or ODS files (typically created using LibreOffice™, Apache OpenOffice™, or other compatible software).

Contributors are encouraged to try to use the correct format when providing their data. However, the data does not have to be in the perfect and final format yet when sharing. The authors of POSTED are happy to help convert data to the correct format.

docs.title: Things to bear in mind
docs.text:
Here is a list of things to bear in mind while collecting data for POSTED and submitting it for inclusion in the public database.

  • What data to include: Generally, the idea is to have relevant data reported in POSTED. This does not mean that the data has to be of high quality. Quality-filtering may happen through selecting data (possibly with masks) using the POSTED framework. If you think that somebody would find the data at hand interesting or relevant for a specific technology or related component, then it can be included. As such, literature that reports certain data but has its focus on very different topics or methods may be included if it is relevant because no other literature reports better data.
  • Report values as the source does: Enter values in the unit, with the reference quantity, and for the year that the source states. Do not convert units, deflate currencies, or rescale to a different plant size by hand. The framework performs these conversions. See Concepts.
  • Document unavoidable conversions: If a value cannot be entered without a manual step, e.g. because a source reports per tonne of steel while the TEDF refers to direct reduced iron, record the assumption and the conversion factor in the comment column.
  • Use reference variables: Report ratios as a variable and a reference variable with separate values and units rather than as a compound unit. A CAPEX of 1000 EUR per kW is entered with value 1000, unit EUR_2020, reference_variable Output Capacity|Hydrogen, reference_value 1, and reference_unit kW.
  • Be precise about provenance: Fill source_detail so that another person can find the number in the source without searching, e.g. the table number, the page, or the spreadsheet cell.
  • Choose the most specific field entry the source supports: A plain value where the case is known, a comma-separated list where a value holds for several cases, the asterisk where it holds for all cases, and N/S only where the source gives no information. See Format.
  • One source per row: If several sources report the same value, enter it once per source.
  • Add the source to sources.bib: Every new source needs a BibTeX entry. Keep the file sorted alphabetically by key and include a DOI, URL, or PDF link where available.

docs.title: Adding a new TEDF
docs.text:
A new technology or variable group is added as a new TEDF. The steps are as follows.

  1. Choose a parent variable, e.g. Tech|My Technology, and create tedfs/Tech/My Technology.csv and tedfs/Tech/My Technology.yaml in the database.
  2. In the metadata file, declare the fields the data needs, reference the variable definitions (predefined: [technology] for technologies), and list the mappings to apply. Copy the metadata of a similar TEDF as a starting point. See Format.
  3. Enter the data in the CSV file following the format.
  4. Add any new sources to sources.bib.
  5. Run the test suite (see below). It validates all TEDFs and runs the full NO-SL-AG workflow on each of them.
  6. For the public database, add a notebook docs/data/My Technology.py in the jupytext percent format that presents the dataset. The existing notebooks serve as templates. The notebooks are executed and converted during the documentation build.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The repository uses uv for environment management and unittest for testing.

uv sync
uv run python -m unittest discover -v

The tests check that every TEDF validates, that the NO-SL-AG workflow runs on every TEDF, and that the source identifiers in the TEDFs and in sources.bib are consistent. Code contributions are additionally checked with ruff.

uv sync --group dev
uv run ruff check ./posted/ ./tests
uv run ruff format --check ./posted/ ./tests/

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is built with mkdocs. The data notebooks are executed before the build.

uv sync --group docs
uv run scripts/register_docs_kernel.py
BUILD_POSTED_DOCS=1 uv run jupytext --to notebook --execute docs/data/*.py
uv run mkdocs serve

docs.title: Contributing code
docs.text: Changes to the framework, e.g. new variable mappings, new field types, or bug fixes, follow the same pull-request procedure. Please open an issue first for larger changes so that the design can be discussed. Code should follow the existing style, pass ruff, and come with a test where feasible.

docs.title: Format
docs.text: This section specifies the files that make up a POSTED database. The ideas behind the data model are explained in Concepts.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
POSTED is extensible via public and private databases. The public database is part of the public GitHub repository (in the posted/database directory) and is installed together with the package. Private project-specific databases can be added to POSTED by adding a respective database path to the databases dictionary before executing any other POSTED code.

from pathlib import Path
from posted import databases

databases |= {"my_private_database": Path("/path/to/database/")}

The public database is intended for the curation of a comprehensive set of general-purpose resources that should suit the needs of most users. Private databases may be used for low-threshold extensibility, for more project-specific work that is not in the interest of a broad audience, or for confidential data that cannot be made available publicly. A TEDF is always loaded from one database, selected by the database_id argument of TEDF.load(), which defaults to "public".

Each database may contain the following components, each contained in a directory or file of the given name.

database/
├── tedfs/                   # techno-economic data files and their metadata
│   ├── Emission Factor.csv
│   ├── Emission Factor.yaml
│   └── Tech/
│       ├── Electrolysis.csv
│       ├── Electrolysis.yaml
│       └── ...
├── variables/
│   ├── definitions/         # reusable variable definitions (YAML)
│   │   └── technology.yaml
│   └── mappings/            # variable mappings (Python)
│       ├── activities.py
│       └── ...
├── masks/                   # default masks per TEDF (YAML)
│   └── Tech/
│       └── Electrolysis.yaml
└── sources.bib              # bibliographic records (BibTeX)
  • tedfs/: This directory contains TEDFs (techno-economic data files), which are UTF-8 encoded CSV files following the format described below. The files are organised in a directory structure that mirrors the hierarchy of variable names. Each TEDF is accompanied by a metadata file in YAML format with the same base name that declares the column structure (fields and comments) and the variables of the file. Both column and variable definitions may be given explicitly or may refer to predefined sets.
  • variables/definitions/: This directory contains variable definitions in YAML format that can be referred to by the metadata files of TEDFs.
  • variables/mappings/: This directory contains variable mappings as Python modules. Mappings transform one representation of a variable into another during the selection step. A TEDF lists the mappings to apply in its metadata file.
  • masks/: This directory contains masks, which assign weights to rows when aggregating data. Masks stored here are applied by default when the corresponding TEDF is aggregated. The directory structure mirrors that of tedfs/.
  • sources.bib: A BibTeX file with one entry per source referenced in the TEDFs of this database.

docs.title: Naming and parent variable
docs.text:
A TEDF consists of a CSV file and a YAML file with the same base name. Its position below tedfs/ defines its parent variable, with directory separators replaced by |. The file tedfs/Tech/Electrolysis.csv has the parent variable Tech|Electrolysis and is loaded with TEDF.load("Tech|Electrolysis"). All variables reported in the file are implicitly prefixed with the parent variable. The variable CAPEX in this file denotes Tech|Electrolysis|CAPEX.

The CSV file is read with , as separator, " as quote character, and UTF-8 encoding. All cells are read as text. Empty cells are permitted only in columns that are not required. The first row holds the column identifiers.

docs.title: Base columns
docs.text:
The TEDF base format contains the following columns. They are present in every TEDF. Columns missing in the CSV file are added as empty columns when the file is read.

Column Required Description source yes A valid BibTeX identifier from the sources.bib file of the database. Exactly one identifier per row. source_detail yes Detailed information on where exactly in the source this entry can be found, e.g. page, table, figure, or spreadsheet cell. variable yes The reported variable, relative to the parent variable. Must be defined in the metadata or in a predefined set under variables/definitions/. reference_variable no The reference variable, relative to the parent variable. Used for variables that are reported in reference to other variables, e.g. CAPEX per rated capacity or energy input per unit of product. value yes The value corresponding to the reported variable. uncertainty no The uncertainty corresponding to the reported variable, in the same unit as the value. unit yes The unit corresponding to the reported variable. Must be a valid unit string known to cet-units. See Units. reference_value no The value corresponding to the reference variable. Only permitted if reference_variable is set. reference_unit no The unit corresponding to the reference variable. Only permitted if reference_variable is set. Must be a valid unit string known to cet-units. comment no A free-text comment on the entry. This column should be used to report any conversion performed if the value originally reported by a source had to be modified before reporting, as well as additional assumptions or deviations from the original units.

The columns source and the fields described below must be filled in every row. The columns source_detail, variable, value, and unit are required as well.

Note: The uncertainty column can currently only be reported but not processed further with the POSTED framework. It is normalised alongside the value and then dropped in the selection step. This feature may be added at a later stage.

Example. The row below reports from a technology catalogue that a 1 MW alkaline electrolyser has a CAPEX of 1566 EUR (2020 prices) per kg of hydrogen output capacity per day in the year 2020, with an uncertainty of 918 EUR.

source,source_detail,subtech,size,period,country,variable,reference_variable,value,uncertainty,unit,reference_value,reference_unit,comment
DEA-TDRF-2023,"Sheet 86 AEC 1MW, Row 24",AEL,1 MW,2020,GLO,CAPEX,Output Capacity|Hydrogen,1566,918,EUR_2020,1,kg_H2/day,

The reference value need not be one. The row below reports that 541 cubic metres of hydrogen are consumed per 1.1 tonnes of direct reduced iron, with the conversion assumption documented in the comment.

Agora-KSV-2023,"Page 79, Tabelle 12",H2,No Capture,Input|Hydrogen,Output|Direct Reduced Iron,2022,#,541,,cubic_meter_H2_norm,1.1,t,"This source states 541 Nm³ of hydrogen per tonne of steel, but does not state how much DRI it assumes per steel. The conversion factor from Devlin et al, 2022 of 1.1 DRI/tSteel is therefore used."

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Fields are additional columns that can help report data that varies across cases or components. Fields can currently be of type case or component.

  • A case field: POSTED treats these columns as different competing options for data. When data is aggregated in the aggregate step of the NO-SL-AG framework, case fields are averaged over.
  • A component field: POSTED treats these columns as components of the same data that require summing up. When data is aggregated in the aggregate step of the NO-SL-AG framework, component fields are simply summed up.

Fields may be coded or non-coded. A coded field defines a fixed set of allowed values (the codes) in the metadata file, and every cell must contain one of these codes or one of the special values below. A non-coded field accepts any text. The source column is a coded case field whose codes are the BibTeX identifiers in sources.bib. The period column is a non-coded case field that accepts integer years.

Two fields are predefined.

  • source is present in every TEDF and does not need to be declared.
  • period must be declared in the metadata file if the TEDF uses it, with the entry period: period. TEDFs without a period column, e.g. emission factors, are permitted. If a TEDF has no period column, selecting by period is not possible.

Field identifiers must not coincide with base column identifiers. Field columns may be placed anywhere in the CSV file. By convention they are placed between source_detail and variable.

docs.title: Field cell values
docs.text:
Every field cell must be filled. Besides a single plain value, the following entries are permitted. How they are processed when selecting data is described in the NO-SL-AG guide.

  • Multiple values (A, B) — A cell may list several comma-separated values if the entry applies equally to each of them. For example, an entry with AEL, PEM in a subtech field reports one value that holds for both alkaline and PEM electrolysis. Spaces around the commas are ignored. This is not available for the source column. Because the comma is the separator, individual values in a multi-value field must not contain commas themselves.
  • Asterisk (*) — The entry applies to all values of this field. Use it when a source reports a value without distinguishing between cases, e.g. a total plant capacity that is the same for every sub-technology, or a parameter that does not depend on the period. The asterisk is a wildcard, not a value of its own. For the period column it is the only permitted non-numeric entry.
  • Not specified (N/S) — The source does not state which value of this field the entry refers to. This differs from the asterisk. The asterisk asserts that the value holds for all cases, whereas N/S records that the case is unknown. It is intended for case fields, e.g. a cost figure from a report that does not mention the plant size.
  • Hash (#) — Only in component fields. It marks an entry that reports the total, i.e. the quantity is not subdivided into components. It is an ordinary value from the point of view of selection and aggregation. Since aggregation sums over all component values within a source and case, a quantity should be reported either as a total with # or itemised by component, never both, as this would double-count.

The asterisk and N/S may be used in any field, including non-coded ones. For coded fields they count as allowed values in addition to the codes. When reporting data, prefer the most specific entry that the source supports: a plain value where the case is known, a comma-separated list where the value is known to hold for several cases, the asterisk where it holds for all cases, and N/S only where the source gives no information.

docs.title: Metadata file
docs.text:
Each TEDF is accompanied by a YAML file with the same base name. It has up to three top-level keys.

columns:
    subtech:
        name: Subtechnology
        description: Subtechnology
        type: case
        coded: True
        codes:
            AEL: Alkaline electrolysis
            PEM: Proton-exchange membrane electrolysis
            SOEC: High-temperature solid-oxide electrolysis
    size:
        name: Plant size
        description: Total size (capacity) of the assumed plant
        type: case
        coded: False
    period: period
variables:
    predefined:
        - technology
mappings:
    - full_load_hours
    - fixed_opex_relative
    - fixed_opex_specific
    - capacities_to_activities
    - activities

columns declares the additional columns of the CSV file. Each key is a column identifier. The value is either the name of a predefined column, currently only period, or a mapping with the following entries.

Entry Required Description type yes case, component, or comment. name yes Human-readable name of the column. description yes Explanation of what the column distinguishes. coded for fields Whether the field only accepts the codes listed under codes. codes if coded Mapping of allowed codes to their descriptions.

Columns of type comment are free-text columns that are carried along with the raw data but dropped during selection, like the base column comment. Columns in the CSV file that are not declared in the metadata are treated as comment columns and a warning is issued.

variables declares the variables that may appear in the variable and reference_variable columns. The entry predefined lists files from variables/definitions/ (without the .yaml extension) whose definitions are included. The entry custom holds definitions written directly in the metadata file, using the same syntax as the definition files. Both may be combined, and later definitions override earlier ones with the same name.

mappings lists the variable mappings from variables/mappings/ (without the .py extension) that are applied during selection, in the given order. Order matters when one mapping depends on the output of another. The standard order for technology TEDFs is shown above and is explained in the NO-SL-AG section.

docs.title: Variable definitions
docs.text:
Variable definitions describe the variables that may appear in TEDFs. They are stored as YAML mappings from variable name to attributes, either in files under variables/definitions/ or under variables: custom: in a metadata file.

CAPEX:
    description: CAPital EXpenditure (in reference to capacity specified by reference variable)
    reference: capacity
    dimension: "[currency]"
    default_unit: "{default currency}"
Input|?flow_type:
    description: Input (energy or feedstock) needed
    reference: activity
    dimension: "[{flow_type_dimension}]"
    default_unit: "{flow_type_default_unit}"
Lifetime:
    description: Expected time a facility can be in production for
    dimension: "[time]"
    default_unit: "a"
Attribute Description description Explanation of the variable. reference How the variable relates to a reference variable. activity for variables reported per unit of a flow, capacity for variables reported per unit of capacity, intensive or absent for variables without a reference. This attribute controls the harmonisation of references during selection. dimension Expected dimensionality of the unit, in pint notation. Documentary; not currently checked by the framework. default_unit Default unit for the variable. Documentary; the framework currently derives target units from the data as described under Units.

Variable names may contain placeholders for name segments. A segment ?name matches exactly one segment of a variable name, e.g. Input|?flow_type matches Input|Electricity and Input|Hydrogen. A segment *name matches the remainder of a variable name including further | separators. Placeholders allow one definition to cover a family of variables.

The public database provides the definition set technology, which covers the variables used by technology TEDFs: CAPEX, OPEX Fixed, OPEX Fixed Specific, OPEX Fixed Relative, OPEX Variable, Lifetime, OCF, FLH, Input|?flow_type, Output|?flow_type, Input Capacity|?flow_type, Output Capacity|?flow_type, Total Input Capacity|?flow_type, Total Output Capacity|?flow_type, Emissions|?emission_type, Capture Rate, and others. The current list is in technology.yaml.

docs.title: Variable mappings
docs.text:
Variable mappings are Python modules in variables/mappings/. Each module defines exactly one class derived from AbstractVariableMapper or AbstractVariableGroupMapper in posted.noslag.mapping. The module name is the identifier used in the mappings list of metadata files.

A mapper implements three methods.

  • _condition() returns a boolean series marking the rows that the mapping applies to.
  • _prepare_units() determines unit conversion factors and registers units for variables that the mapping creates. Optional.
  • _map(df, cond) transforms the marked rows and returns the modified frame. For AbstractVariableMapper it is called once for the whole frame. For AbstractVariableGroupMapper it is called once per combination of field values, which allows a mapping to use other variables of the same source and case, e.g. the CAPEX belonging to a relative OPEX.

A mapper may declare _warning_types, a mapping of warning identifiers to messages, and call _add_warning() to flag rows that could not be mapped. Such rows are reported to the user and dropped. The simplest mapping in the public database converts full-load hours into a capacity factor.

"""Convert full-load hours to operational capacity factor."""

import pandas as pd
from cet_units import Q

from posted.noslag.mapping import AbstractVariableMapper


class FullLoadHoursMapper(AbstractVariableMapper):
    """Convert full-load hours to operational capacity factor."""

    def _condition(self) -> pd.Series:
        return self._df["variable"] == "FLH"

    def _prepare_units(self) -> None:
        if "OCF" not in self._units:
            self._units["OCF"] = "dimensionless"
        self._conv_factor: float = (
            (Q(self._units["FLH"]) / Q("year")).to(self._units["OCF"]).m
        )

    def _map(self, df: pd.DataFrame, cond: pd.Series) -> pd.DataFrame:
        df.loc[cond, "variable"] = "OCF"
        df.loc[cond, "value"] *= self._conv_factor

        return df

The mapper receives the frame with the columns variable, reference_variable, and value, a dictionary of target units per variable, the row groups, the patterns of activity-type and capacity-type variables, and the reference activity and reference capacity. The mappings shipped with the public database are described in the NO-SL-AG section.

docs.title: Masks
docs.text:
Default masks for a TEDF are stored in masks/ under the same relative path as the TEDF, e.g. masks/Tech/Electrolysis.yaml for tedfs/Tech/Electrolysis.csv. The file holds a list of mask specifications. Each specification is passed to the constructor of posted.noslag.Mask.

- where: "variable == 'CAPEX'"
  use: "source == 'Example-2020'"
  weight: nan
  other: 1.0
  comment: CAPEX in this source is misquoted from another publication.
Key Description where Condition or list of conditions that all rows of a group must satisfy for the mask to apply to that group. use Condition or list of conditions identifying rows that receive a weight. weight Weight or list of weights, one per use condition. Defaults to 1. A weight of nan excludes the row. other Weight for rows of the group that match none of the use conditions. Defaults to nan, i.e. such rows are excluded. comment Free-text explanation.

Conditions are strings evaluated with DataFrame.eval() on the selected data, mappings of column to value that must all be equal, or callables that receive a row and return a boolean. The variable column at that stage does not include the parent variable. The semantics of masks during aggregation are described in the NO-SL-AG section.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Sources are stored in sources.bib in BibTeX format. The BibTeX key is the identifier used in the source column of all TEDFs of the database. Keys in the public database follow the pattern Author-Year or Institution-Acronym-Year, e.g. Vartiainen-2022 or DEA-TDRF-2023.

The following rules are enforced by the test suite of the public database.

  • Every identifier used in a TEDF must have an entry in sources.bib.
  • Every entry in sources.bib must be used in at least one TEDF.
  • Entries must be sorted alphabetically by key, case-insensitively.
  • Every entry must be parseable and formattable by pybtex.

In addition to standard BibTeX fields, the non-standard field pdf may hold a direct link to a PDF file. It is used alongside doi and url to generate the links on the Sources page.

Only one source may belong to a row of data. If the same value is reported by several sources, it is entered once per source on separate rows.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
POSTED requires Python 3.11 or 3.12. The package can be installed via pip directly from GitHub.

pip install git+https://github.com/PhilippVerpoort/posted.git

To install a specific release, append the tag name.

pip install git+https://github.com/PhilippVerpoort/posted.git@v0.6.0

Alternatively, clone the repository and install it locally. This is the recommended way for contributors.

git clone https://github.com/PhilippVerpoort/posted.git
cd posted
pip install -e .

The project uses uv for dependency management. Contributors can set up the development environment with uv sync --group dev and the documentation environment with uv sync --group docs.

The public database is shipped as part of the package, so no separate download of data is required.

Note: The package will be published on PyPI in the near future for simpler installation.

docs.title: Loading a TEDF
docs.text:
Each techno-economic data file (TEDF) is identified by its parent variable, which corresponds to its path in the database. The TEDF for water electrolysis is located at tedfs/Tech/Electrolysis.csv and has the parent variable Tech|Electrolysis.

from posted import TEDF

tedf = TEDF.load("Tech|Electrolysis")

The raw data can be inspected as a pandas DataFrame. It contains the values as reported by the sources.

tedf.raw

The fields of the TEDF, i.e. the columns that distinguish cases and components, are described in its metadata.

for field_id, field in tedf.fields.items():
    print(field_id, field.field_type, field.codes)

docs.title: Harmonising data
docs.text:
The three steps of the NO-SL-AG workflow are available as methods of the TEDF class. Each step includes the previous ones, so a single call is sufficient.

# Convert all entries to common units and reference values.
normalised = tedf.normalise()

# Additionally select cases, harmonise variables, and interpolate periods.
selected = tedf.select(period=[2030, 2040], subtech=["AEL", "PEM"])

# Additionally average over sources and sum over components.
aggregated = tedf.aggregate(period=[2030, 2040], subtech=["AEL", "PEM"])

The arguments period and subtech refer to fields of the electrolysis TEDF. Any field can be used as a keyword argument to restrict the selection. Fields that are omitted are selected in full. The NO-SL-AG section explains the behaviour of each step and all available arguments in detail.

The result of aggregate() is a tidy DataFrame with one row per remaining case and variable. For the call above, the columns are the fields subtech, size, country, and period, followed by variable, reference_variable, value, unit, and reference_unit. Sources have been averaged over, so no source column remains (source is the only aggregation field by default; other aggregation options can be chosen via arguments).

aggregated.query("variable == 'CAPEX'")

docs.title: Choosing units and references
docs.text:
By default, the framework chooses the most common unit per variable found in the data, with currencies converted to the default currency. Units can be overridden per variable, and the reference quantities for activity-type and capacity-type variables can be set explicitly.

aggregated = tedf.aggregate(
    period=[2030],
    units={"CAPEX": "EUR_2024", "Output|Hydrogen": "MWh_H2_LHV"},
    reference_capacity="Output Capacity|Hydrogen",
    reference_activity="Output|Hydrogen",
)

See Units for the unit notation and Concepts for the role of reference variables.

docs.title: Changing defaults
docs.text:
The default period and the default currency are stored in a dictionary that can be modified before data is processed.

import posted

posted.defaults["period"] = [2030]
posted.defaults["currency"] = "USD_2022"

docs.title: Registering a private database
docs.text:
Project-specific or confidential data can be kept in a private database with the same structure as the public one. It is registered by adding its path to the databases dictionary.

from pathlib import Path
import posted

posted.databases["my_project"] = Path("/path/to/my_database")

tedf = TEDF.load("Tech|My Technology", database_id="my_project")

The structure of a database is described in the Format section.

docs.title: Validating data
docs.text:
A TEDF can be checked for formal consistency, e.g. valid units, numeric values, allowed field codes, and known source identifiers.

tedf.validate()
tedf.validated  # DataFrame of booleans, one per cell

This check is also run by the test suite for all TEDFs in the public database.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Concepts explains the data model behind TEDFs.
  • Format specifies the files of a database.
  • NO-SL-AG describes the harmonisation workflow in detail.
  • The Data section shows the content of each TEDF in the public database.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Activity-type variable A variable that describes a flow or cost during operation and is reported relative to another flow, e.g. electricity input per unit of hydrogen output. Declared with reference: activity in the variable definitions. See Concepts. Aggregate The third step of NO-SL-AG. Sums over component fields, averages over case fields, and applies masks. See NO-SL-AG. Asterisk (*) Field entry meaning that a value applies to all values of the field. Expanded to all requested values during selection. See Format. Base column One of the columns present in every TEDF: source, source_detail, variable, reference_variable, value, uncertainty, unit, reference_value, reference_unit, and comment. See Format. Capacity-type variable A variable tied to the installed plant and reported relative to a capacity, e.g. CAPEX per unit of output capacity. Declared with reference: capacity in the variable definitions. Case field A field whose values are competing alternatives, e.g. sub-technologies or years. Averaged over when aggregated. See Concepts. Coded field A field with a fixed set of allowed values (codes) defined in the metadata file. Component field A field whose values are parts that add up to a whole, e.g. cost items. Summed over when aggregated. Database A directory containing TEDFs, metadata, variable definitions, mappings, masks, and sources. POSTED ships a public database and can register private ones. See Format. Field An additional column of a TEDF that distinguishes cases or components. Defined in the metadata file of the TEDF. Hash (#) Entry in a component field marking a total that is not subdivided into components. Harmonised data Output of the NO-SL-AG workflow in which all values of a variable share one unit and one reference. See Concepts. Mask A rule that assigns weights to rows matching a condition during aggregation. Used to exclude or weight entries. See NO-SL-AG. Metadata file The YAML file accompanying each TEDF. Declares fields, comment columns, variable definitions, and mappings. See Format. Normalise The first step of NO-SL-AG. Converts units, deflates currencies, and scales values to reference values of one. See NO-SL-AG. NO-SL-AG The normalise, select, aggregate workflow for converting raw data into harmonised data. Also written NOSLAG. Not specified (N/S) Field entry meaning that the source does not state which value of the field an entry refers to. Parent variable The leading part of a variable name that is given by the position of a TEDF in the database, e.g. Tech|Electrolysis. Used to load a TEDF. Period Predefined case field holding the year a value refers to. Supports interpolation and extrapolation. Raw data The data as entered in a TEDF, in the units and references of the original source. Reference activity, reference capacity The common reference variables onto which all activity-type and capacity-type variables are rebased during selection. Reference variable The denominator of a reported ratio, e.g. Output Capacity|Hydrogen for a CAPEX value. Has its own value and unit. Select The second step of NO-SL-AG. Filters and expands fields, interpolates periods, and applies variable mappings. See NO-SL-AG. Source The publication a value is taken from, identified by a BibTeX key from sources.bib. Treated as a case field. TEDF Techno-economic data file. A CSV file with one row per reported value, accompanied by a metadata file. See Format. Variable The name of the reported quantity, e.g. CAPEX or Input|Electricity. Hierarchical, with segments separated by |. Variable definition An entry describing a variable, including its relation to a reference (activity, capacity, or intensive), its dimension, and its default unit. Stored in variables/definitions/ or in the metadata file. Variable mapping Code in variables/mappings/ that converts one form of a variable into another during selection, e.g. full-load hours into a capacity factor. See NO-SL-AG.

docs.title: NO-SL-AG
docs.text:
NO-SL-AG (also written NOSLAG) stands for normalise, select, aggregate. It is the workflow that converts the raw data of a TEDF into harmonised data. The three steps are implemented as methods of the TEDF class and build on each other: select() begins by normalising, and aggregate() begins by selecting. Users typically call only the method whose output they need.

Step Method Purpose Output Normalise TEDF.normalise() Common units, deflated currencies, reference values of one Raw data with converted values, same columns as the TEDF Select TEDF.select() Resolve fields, pick cases, interpolate periods, harmonise variables and references One row per source, case, component, and variable Aggregate TEDF.aggregate() Sum over components, weighted average over sources and other cases One row per remaining case and variable

Throughout this section, examples use the electrolysis TEDF with the fields subtech, size, country, and period, and the direct-reduction TEDF with the fields carbon_capture, mode, component, and period.

docs.title: Normalise
docs.text:
Normalisation makes values from different sources numerically comparable without changing what they represent. It performs the following operations on every row.

  1. Parse numbers. The value, uncertainty, and reference_value columns are converted to floating-point numbers. Empty cells become missing values.
  2. Determine target units. One target unit is assigned to each variable, whether it appears in the variable or the reference_variable column. The procedure is described under Units: currencies are rewritten to the default currency, the most frequent unit is chosen, and entries in the units argument override the choice.
  3. Convert units. For each row, the value is multiplied by the conversion factor from the reported unit to the target unit of its variable, and divided by the conversion factor from the reported reference unit to the target unit of its reference variable. Currency conversion includes deflation between base years.
  4. Scale to a reference value of one. The value is divided by the reference value, so that every row expresses the variable per one unit of its reference variable. The uncertainty is scaled by the same factor.
  5. Write back. The unit and reference_unit columns hold the target units, and reference_value holds one for all rows with a reference variable.

The output of normalise() has the same columns as the raw TEDF, including fields and comment columns, and the same number of rows. A row that reports 1566 EUR_2020 per 1 kg_H2/day thus becomes a row reporting 1884 EUR_2024 per 1 kg_H2/day if the default currency is EUR_2024 and the most frequent reference unit is kg_H2/day.

tedf.normalise()
tedf.normalise(units={"CAPEX": "USD_2022", "Output Capacity|Hydrogen": "kW_H2_LHV"})

Normalisation does not change which rows exist, what the variables are called, or which reference variable each row uses. These aspects are handled by the selection step.

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
Selection turns normalised data into a consistent set of rows for the cases a user is interested in. It consists of the following stages, applied in order.

  1. Drop auxiliary columns. The uncertainty column and all comment columns (source_detail, comment, custom comment columns) are removed.
  2. Resolve fields. For each field, special cell values are expanded and the requested values are kept. The period field is resolved last, because it may involve interpolation. This stage is described in detail below.
  3. Check for duplicates. After expansion, each combination of field values, variable, and reference variable must occur only once. Otherwise an exception is raised.
  4. Drop singular fields. Fields with fewer than two distinct values in the result are removed, unless drop_singular_fields=False. This includes source and period. For instance, if only the year 2030 is requested, the period column does not appear in the output.
  5. Determine reference activity and reference capacity. Unless given as arguments, the reference activity is the most frequent reference variable among activity-type variables in the raw data, and the reference capacity is the most frequent reference variable among capacity-type variables.
  6. Apply variable mappings. The mappings listed in the metadata file are applied in order. Rows that a mapping could not process are reported as warnings and dropped.
  7. Check reference variables. Every variable must have exactly one reference variable in the result. Otherwise an exception is raised.
  8. Finalise. The unit and reference_unit columns are added. If with_parent=True, the parent variable is prepended to variable names. If append_references=True, reference variables are added as rows with value one instead of being listed in separate columns.

The output has one row per source, case, component, and variable, with the columns source, the remaining fields, variable, reference_variable, value, unit, and reference_unit.

tedf.select(period=[2030, 2050], subtech=["AEL", "PEM"], size="100 MW")

docs.title: Field selection and expansion
docs.text:
The select() and aggregate() methods of TEDF accept one keyword argument per field, e.g. select(subtech=["AEL", "PEM"], period=[2030, 2040]). For each field, the framework first expands the special cell values described in the format guide and then keeps the rows that match the requested values.

Requested values. If a field is given as an argument, the listed values are requested. A single value is accepted in place of a list. If a field is omitted, all values that occur in that column of the TEDF are requested, after splitting comma-separated cells. The asterisk and N/S do not count as values here. The period field is the exception: when omitted, the default period from posted.defaults is requested instead of all observed years. The asterisk itself must not be passed as a requested value; omit the argument instead. Passing a keyword argument that is not a field of the TEDF raises an exception.

Comma-separated cells are split into one row per value before selection. An entry with AEL, PEM therefore behaves like two identical entries, one for AEL and one for PEM.

Asterisk. Each row with * is replaced by one copy per requested value. If subtech=["AEL"] is requested, a * row becomes a single AEL row. If the field is omitted, the row is copied once for each value observed in the column. The asterisk never expands to N/S unless N/S is requested explicitly.

Not specified. The treatment of N/S depends on the expand_not_specified argument.

  • True (default): N/S is converted to * before expansion and therefore behaves like the asterisk. The value is then available for every requested case, and N/S does not appear in the output.
  • False: N/S is kept as a field value of its own. Rows with N/S are returned alongside the other values when the field is omitted, and can be requested explicitly, e.g. size=["N/S"]. Asterisk rows are not expanded to N/S in this case.
  • A list of field names: N/S is expanded only in the listed fields and kept in all others.

Expanding N/S is convenient when the unspecified entries should contribute to all cases, for instance when a source reports a cost without stating the plant size and this cost is to be averaged with size-specific costs from other sources. Keeping N/S is preferable when unspecified entries should be inspected or filtered separately.

Hash. The # entry of component fields is not expanded. It is an ordinary field value that labels the undivided total. During aggregation, all component values of a source and case are summed, including #.

Duplicates. After expansion, each combination of source, field values, variable, and reference variable must occur only once. A TEDF that reports the same variable from the same source both with * and with an explicit value for the same field therefore raises an error during selection. Contributors should report either the wildcard or the explicit cases, not both.

Example. Consider a size field with the entries below and no size argument.

entry expanded with expand_not_specified=True expanded with expand_not_specified=False 1 MW 1 MW 1 MW 1 MW, 100 MW 1 MW, 100 MW 1 MW, 100 MW * 1 MW, 100 MW, 5 MW 1 MW, 100 MW, 5 MW N/S 1 MW, 100 MW, 5 MW N/S 5 MW 5 MW 5 MW

docs.title: Periods
docs.text:
The period field is a case field with numeric values, which allows values to be estimated for years that no source reports. After the asterisk has been expanded and the column has been converted to integers, the rows are grouped by all other columns, i.e. by source, remaining fields, variable, and reference variable. Within each group, the requested periods are served as follows, depending on the period_mode argument.

period_mode Requested year is reported Requested year lies between reported years Requested year lies outside reported years "none" kept dropped dropped "inter" kept linear interpolation between the nearest reported years dropped "extra" kept dropped value of the nearest reported year "inter+extra" (default) kept linear interpolation value of the nearest reported year

Extrapolation is constant, i.e. a projection for 2050 is carried forward unchanged to 2060. Interpolation and extrapolation are performed per source. If a source reports only one year, that value is used for all requested years in the extrapolating modes. The values PeriodMode.NONE, PeriodMode.INTERPOLATE, PeriodMode.EXTRAPOLATE, and PeriodMode.INTER_AND_EXTRAPOLATION from posted._columns.fields may be passed instead of the strings.

If no period argument is given, the default period posted.defaults["period"], which is [2025] unless changed, is requested. To obtain all reported years without interpolation, pass the observed years explicitly together with period_mode="none".

docs.title: Reference activity and reference capacity
docs.text:
Within one TEDF, sources refer their data to different quantities. One source reports CAPEX per unit of hydrogen output capacity, another per unit of electrical input capacity. One source reports electricity demand per unit of hydrogen, another reports hydrogen output per unit of electricity. Harmonised data needs a single convention.

The selection step establishes one reference activity for all activity-type variables and one reference capacity for all capacity-type variables. Which variables count as activity-type or capacity-type is declared in the variable definitions through the reference attribute. By default, the references are the most frequent reference variables of their kind in the raw data. They can be set explicitly through the arguments reference_activity and reference_capacity.

tedf.select(
    reference_activity="Output|Hydrogen",
    reference_capacity="Output Capacity|Hydrogen",
)

Rebasing data onto these references is performed by the variable mappings described next.

docs.title: Variable mappings
docs.text:
Variable mappings transform rows during selection. They are stored as Python modules in the database and are listed per TEDF in its metadata file. The mappings of the public database, in the order in which technology TEDFs apply them, are the following.

Mapping Transforms Into Notes full_load_hours FLH (full-load hours per year) OCF (operational capacity factor) Division by one year. fixed_opex_relative OPEX Fixed Relative (share of CAPEX per year) OPEX Fixed per unit of capacity Needs CAPEX from the same source and case. Warns and drops the row otherwise. fixed_opex_specific OPEX Fixed Specific (per unit of product) OPEX Fixed per unit of capacity Divides by the OCF of the same source and case. Assumes an OCF of 100% with a warning if none or several are found. capacities_to_activities Ratios of two capacities, e.g. Input Capacity|Electricity per Output Capacity|Hydrogen Ratios of the corresponding activities, e.g. Input|Electricity per Output|Hydrogen Multiplies both sides by one year. activities All activity-type rows whose reference differs from the reference activity, and all capacity-type rows whose reference differs from the reference capacity Rows expressed relative to the reference activity and reference capacity See below.

The activities mapping is the central harmonisation step. For each source and case, it collects all activity-type rows, e.g. electricity input per hydrogen output and hydrogen output per electricity input, and solves the resulting system of linear relations for the ratio of every flow to the reference activity. A row whose variable is the reference activity itself is inverted, so that Output|Hydrogen per Input|Electricity becomes Input|Electricity per Output|Hydrogen. Capacity-type rows are rescaled with the same ratios, so that CAPEX per hydrogen output capacity becomes CAPEX per electricity input capacity if the latter is the reference capacity. Variables of the form Total Input Capacity|X and Total Output Capacity|X are converted to the total of the reference capacity. If a source does not provide the ratios needed to connect a row to the reference, the row cannot be rebased. It is reported in a warning and dropped.

Group-wise mappings operate on groups formed by all fields that remain after singular fields are dropped. This includes component fields. A relative OPEX reported for one component is therefore matched with the CAPEX of the same component only.

docs.title: Aggregate
docs.text:
Aggregation condenses the selected data to one value per case and variable. It proceeds as follows.

  1. Select. The selection step is run with the same arguments.
  2. Collect masks. Masks from the database for this TEDF are combined with masks passed in the masks argument. Database masks can be excluded with masks_database=False.
  3. Determine fields to aggregate. The agg argument lists the fields to aggregate over. By default, these are all component fields and source. Case fields other than source are not aggregated unless listed.
  4. Sum over components. For component fields in agg, values are summed within each combination of the remaining columns. A source reporting labour and maintenance as separate components of fixed OPEX thus contributes their sum.
  5. Average over cases. For each combination of the remaining columns, the rows that differ only in the aggregated case fields are combined. Every row starts with a weight of one. Each mask whose where conditions hold for the group multiplies the weights by the weights it assigns. Rows with an undefined weight are dropped. The remaining rows are combined by a weighted arithmetic mean.
  6. Finalise. As for selection: units are added, the parent variable is optionally prepended, and reference variables are optionally appended as rows.
# Default: sum over components, average over sources.
tedf.aggregate(period=[2030])

# Additionally average over plant sizes.
tedf.aggregate(period=[2030], agg=["source", "size"])

# Keep sources and components; only apply masks and reshape.
tedf.aggregate(period=[2030], agg=[])

The arithmetic mean is a deliberate default. Alternative aggregation statistics, e.g. the median, are not currently supported. Weighting through masks allows the influence of individual sources to be adjusted.

The output has one row per remaining case and variable, with the remaining fields followed by variable, reference_variable, value, unit, and reference_unit. If no rows remain, an empty frame with these columns is returned.

docs.title: Masks
docs.text:
A mask is an object of class posted.noslag.Mask with the following parts.

  • where: one or more conditions that every row of a group must satisfy for the mask to apply to that group. Groups are formed by the columns that are not aggregated over, so a where condition typically restricts the variable or a case field, e.g. "variable == 'CAPEX'".
  • use: one or more conditions that identify rows within the group, e.g. "source == 'Example-2020'".
  • weight: one weight per use condition. Defaults to one.
  • other: the weight for rows that match none of the use conditions. Defaults to nan, which excludes those rows.

Weights of several applicable masks are multiplied. A row with a weight of nan is excluded from the average. A mask with only a use condition and the default other therefore acts as a filter that keeps only the matching rows. A mask with weight: nan and other: 1.0 excludes the matching rows and keeps the rest. Conditions may be given as strings for DataFrame.eval(), as dictionaries mapping columns to required values, or as callables applied to each row.

from posted.noslag import Mask

# Exclude the CAPEX values of one source, keep everything else.
exclude = Mask(
    where="variable == 'CAPEX'",
    use="source == 'Example-2020'",
    weight=float("nan"),
    other=1.0,
)

# Give one source twice the weight of the others.
emphasise = Mask(use="source == 'DEA-TDRF-2023'", weight=2.0, other=1.0)

tedf.aggregate(period=[2030], masks=[exclude, emphasise])

Masks stored in the masks/ directory of a database are loaded automatically with the TEDF and applied by default. Their file format is described in the Format section.

docs.title: Appending references
docs.text:
By default, the output lists the reference variable and its unit in separate columns. Some downstream tools prefer every quantity as a row of its own. With append_references=True, the reference columns are omitted and each reference variable is added as a row with the value one for every combination of remaining field values.

tedf.aggregate(period=[2030], append_references=True)

The resulting rows state, for instance, that Input Capacity|Electricity equals 1 kW and CAPEX equals 700 EUR_2024, which together express a CAPEX of 700 EUR per kW.

docs.title: Argument reference
docs.text:
The arguments below are shared by select() and aggregate() unless noted otherwise. normalise() accepts only units and with_parent.

Argument Default Description units None Mapping of variable names to target units. Overrides the automatic choice. reference_activity most frequent in data Reference variable for all activity-type variables. reference_capacity most frequent in data Reference variable for all capacity-type variables. drop_singular_fields True Remove fields with fewer than two distinct values from the output. period_mode "inter+extra" Treatment of requested years that are not reported. See Periods. expand_not_specified True Whether N/S behaves like the asterisk. May be a list of field names. with_parent False Prepend the parent variable to variable names in the output. append_references False Add reference variables as rows with value one instead of columns. agg component fields and source Fields to aggregate over. aggregate() only. masks None Additional masks to apply. aggregate() only. masks_database True Whether to apply the masks stored in the database. aggregate() only. **field_vals_select all values, period from defaults One keyword per field with the values to select.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
POSTED is aimed at researchers who perform techno-economic assessments or modelling exercises in the context of the energy transition, industrial ecology, climate mitigation, and related fields.

Such work relies on techno-economic parameters, i.e. a combination of technological parameters (concerning the physical performance of a technology, such as energy demand or conversion efficiency) and economic parameters (concerning its cost of investment and operation). Other relevant parameters include market prices, technology lifetimes, or emission intensities.

This data is compartmentalised and scattered across many sources (academic literature, grey literature, technical reports, databases of public agencies, etc). Collecting it for an analysis, tracing its origin transparently, and harmonising it consistently is a cumbersome and error-prone endeavour that is repeated by many research groups in parallel.

POSTED addresses this problem with two components.

  • A public database of techno-economic data, curated as a set of techno-economic data files (TEDFs) that record values as they are reported in the original sources.
  • A Python framework that converts this raw data into harmonised, analysis-ready data in a reproducible way. The central part of this framework is the NO-SL-AG (normalise, select, aggregate) workflow.

The POSTED database and framework aim to achieve the following.

  • Curate a comprehensive collection of techno-economic data to relieve researchers from performing this task manually for each analysis.
  • Store this data in a machine-readable format to ease interoperability.
  • Transparently report where original data can be found to make research and its assumptions understandable and reproducible.
  • Simplify the conversion of raw data into specific formats to ease further processing in other tools.
  • Avoid misunderstandings when storing and reading data through the development and explication of clear standards.
  • Be extendable to meet a variety of requirements by different user groups.

In particular, POSTED aspires to comply with the FAIR principles of research data.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
Three principles shape the design of POSTED. They are explained in more detail in the Concepts section.

Report data as found in the source, harmonise in code. A TEDF records each value with the unit, the reference quantity, and the period stated by the original source. No manual unit conversion, currency deflation, or rescaling takes place when data is entered. All of these transformations are performed by the framework when the data is read. This separation keeps the database transparent and auditable: every number in a TEDF can be checked against its source, and every transformation is documented in code rather than in the heads of contributors.

Make the structure of the data explicit. Techno-economic data varies along several dimensions: across sources, across variants of a technology (sub-technologies, plant sizes, operation modes), across time, and across sub-components of a cost or energy demand. POSTED represents each of these dimensions as a column of the TEDF with a defined type. The type determines how the framework treats the dimension when selecting and aggregating data, for instance whether values are averaged or summed.

Separate data collection from data judgement. Values from sources of varying quality can coexist in the database. Whether a value is used in a specific analysis is decided when the data is selected and aggregated, for instance by restricting to specific sources or by applying masks that weight or exclude entries. Contributors are not required to judge the quality of a source before adding its data.

docs.title: Components at a glance
docs.text: Component What it is Where to read more Database A directory with TEDFs, their metadata, variable definitions, variable mappings, masks, and a BibTeX file of sources. POSTED ships a public database and can register private ones. Format TEDF A techno-economic data file: a CSV file plus a YAML metadata file describing one technology or one group of related variables. Format Variables Named quantities such as CAPEX or Input|Electricity. Many variables are reported relative to a reference variable, e.g. CAPEX per unit of output capacity. Concepts Fields Additional columns that distinguish cases (competing alternatives, averaged over) and components (parts of a whole, summed up). Concepts NO-SL-AG The three-step workflow normalise, select, aggregate that turns raw data into harmonised data. NO-SL-AG Units Unit handling, including flow-specific units and currencies with base years, via the cet-units package. Units Sources Bibliographic records in BibTeX format referenced from every row of data. Format

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
A typical workflow looks like this.

  1. Find techno-economic data in an original source, e.g. an academic journal article or a technical report.
  2. Record this data in a TEDF in its original form (unit, reference quantity, period, etc). TEDFs are UTF-8 encoded comma-separated value (CSV) files. See Format.
  3. Normalise the data alongside data from other sources to common units and reference values using TEDF.normalise(). See NO-SL-AG.
  4. Select the cases and components required for the analysis, e.g. a specific year or sub-technology, using TEDF.select(). This step also harmonises variables, e.g. by expressing all energy inputs relative to the same output. See NO-SL-AG.
  5. Aggregate the data over sources, cases, or components using TEDF.aggregate(). See NO-SL-AG.
  6. Use the resulting harmonised data as input for further processing in other tools.

Steps 3 to 5 build on each other: select() runs normalise() internally and aggregate() runs select() internally. Users therefore typically call only one of the three methods.

For a hands-on introduction, continue with Getting Started. For the ideas behind the data model, continue with Concepts.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: POSTED does not implement its own unit system. It relies on cet-units, a unit registry for climate, energy, and technology applications that extends the pint library. Every unit string in a TEDF must be understood by this registry. This page summarises the parts of the notation that matter for POSTED. The full documentation is available on the cet-units website.

docs.title: Plain units
docs.text:
Standard physical units and SI prefixes are available as in pint, e.g. kW, MWh, GJ, t, kg, hour, day. Compound units use / and *, e.g. t/year or kg_H2/day.

The units a, year, and yr are synonyms. For convenience, one year is defined as 365 days in cet-units. Capacities given per year and per hour can therefore be converted exactly.

Percentages are written as percent or pct and are dimensionless. A value of 90 with unit percent is converted to 0.9 when the target unit is dimensionless.

docs.title: Flow units
docs.text:
Flows such as hydrogen, ammonia, or natural gas can be quantified by mass, volume, or energy content. cet-units provides flow-specific units that encode the substance as a suffix, which allows conversion between these dimensions.

Notation Meaning Example kg_H2, t_NH3 Mass of the flow kg_H2 cubic_meter_H2_norm Volume of the flow at normal conditions cubic_meter_NG_norm MWh_H2_LHV, GJ_NG_HHV Energy content based on lower (LHV) or higher (HHV) heating value kWh_MeOH_LHV kW_NH3_LHV Energy flow rate based on heating value kW_MeOH_LHV

A quantity of 1 kg_H2 can be converted to MWh_H2_LHV, and a hydrogen capacity of 1 kg_H2/day to kW_H2_LHV. Conversion between different flows is not possible.

The flows available by default in cet-units can be extended. POSTED registers the following additional flow identifiers when it is imported: crude_oil, coal, CH4, H2, H2O, MeOH, NG, NH3, O2.

Where a TEDF column refers to a flow without a flow-specific unit, e.g. MWh for electricity or t for cement, the plain unit is used. In that case, conversion between dimensions is not available and all sources must report the quantity in the same dimension.

docs.title: Currencies
docs.text:
Currencies are written with a base year, e.g. EUR_2020 or USD_2023. cet-units converts between base years by deflation and between currencies by exchange rate. Prefixes are permitted, e.g. MEUR_2018 or kUSD_2022. A currency without a year is not a valid unit in POSTED.

Costs that recur annually use a time unit in the denominator, e.g. EUR_2020/year for fixed OPEX. Investment costs do not, e.g. EUR_2020 for CAPEX.

docs.title: Default units and overrides
docs.text:
The normalisation step of NO-SL-AG assigns one target unit to each variable in the following way.

  1. All units found for the variable are collected, both from the unit column where the variable is reported and from the reference_unit column where it serves as a reference.
  2. Currency units are rewritten to the default currency given by posted.defaults["currency"], which is EUR_2024 unless changed.
  3. The most frequent unit among the rewritten units is chosen as the target unit.
  4. Entries in the units argument of normalise(), select(), or aggregate() override the automatic choice for the given variables.

The units argument maps variable names, without the parent variable, to unit strings.

tedf.aggregate(
    units={
        "CAPEX": "EUR_2024",
        "Output Capacity|Hydrogen": "kW_H2_LHV",
        "Input|Electricity": "MWh",
    }
)

Because the automatic choice follows the data, the output units can change when new data is added to a TEDF. Analyses that depend on specific units should set them explicitly.

Variable mappings may introduce variables that are not present in the raw data, e.g. OPEX Fixed derived from OPEX Fixed Relative. Their units are derived from the units of the variables they are computed from. They can also be set through the units argument.

docs.title: Dimension checks
docs.text: The metadata of variable definitions in the database records a dimension and a default unit for each variable, e.g. [currency] for CAPEX or [time] for lifetime. These entries document the expected dimensionality of a variable. At present, the framework does not check reported units against them. The validation step only checks that each unit string is known to the unit registry.
